title: Runtime trace scripts and debugging runbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a working runbook and collection of small scripts intended to standardize how we collect, upload, and triage runtime traces for latency regressions and throughput anomalies in the serving runtime. Focus is on low-latency token generation paths (KV cache, autoregressive decode), batching behavior, and kernel hotspots when running on GPU-backed Dedicated hosts.

Scope and assumptions:
- Targets: redwood-serving (go/python runtime processes) and the GPU worker containers we run in Dedicated and Private.
- We assume debug-symbols or at least existence of address-to-symbol maps for native libs used by kernels (e.g., fused-attn).
- This doc mixes quick triage steps (for oncall) and deeper profiling instructions (for engineers).

Quick triage checklist (oncall):
1) Gather baseline logs and metrics (first 5 minutes):
   - Pull request logs: k8s pod logs (kubectl -n reworker logs -f <pod>)
   - Console traces: request ids, route, model, seq_len, batch size, kv_cache_hit
   - Metrics: per-route p50/p95 latency, GPU utilization, GPU mem, host CPU, ock (use grafana snapshot)
2) Run lightweight wall-clock tracer (30s):
   - On node: sudo ./trace-collect.sh <pod> 30s output.tar.gz
   - Upload artifact to S3: ./upload-artifact.sh output.tar.gz s3://perf-traces/<incident-id>/
3) If CPU is pegged >90% and GPU idle: collect per-thread CPU stacks (py-spy / go pprof)
4) If GPU is saturated or OOM-ing: collect nvprof/Nsight system trace (see below)

Common quick findings and likely causes:
- Spiky p95 but stable p50: batching / queueing depth variability (investigate batch scheduling and backpressure).
- High CPU + low GPU: tokenization, JSON path or request parsing, runtime scheduling overhead (pin threads, check cgroup cpuset).
- High GPU mem + OOMs: batch sizing + KV cache growth, quantization fallback causing larger memory working set.

Trace collection script (trace-collect.sh) — copy this snippet into the node or toolbox image:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Minimal collector: samples perf, pprof endpoints, and gpu counters.
DURATION=${1:-30}
OUT=${2:-trace-$(date +%s).tar.gz}
POD=${3:-}
# 1) Snapshot logs
kubectl -n reworker logs ${POD} --tail=500 > /tmp/pod-logs.txt || true
# 2) Query /debug/pprof endpoints if present
for ep in cpu profile heap goroutine; do
  curl -sS "http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/$ep?seconds=$DURATION" -o /tmp/pprof-$ep || true
done
# 3) perf record (sample, user+kernel stacks)
sudo perf record -F 250 -a -g -- sleep $DURATION || true
sudo perf script > /tmp/perf-unfolded.txt || true
# 4) nvtx + nvidia-smi polling for GPU nodes
which nvidia-smi >/dev/null 2>&1 && (nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,memory.used --format=csv -l 1 -f /tmp/gpu-stats.txt & pid=$!; sleep $DURATION; kill $pid) || true
# 5) Package artifacts
tar -czf $OUT /tmp/pprof-* /tmp/perf-unfolded.txt /tmp/pod-logs.txt /tmp/gpu-stats.txt || true
echo "collected $OUT"

Notes on running system-level profilers:
- perf sampling frequency: 250Hz is a good starting point; reduce for low-impact sampling or increase for short bursts. Make sure kernel.perf_event_paranoid is <=1 on nodes used for perf.
- perf needs debug packages for user-space symbolization. If symbols are stripped, collect build id maps (eu-readelf) or upload the binary.
- For Python-heavy stacks use py-spy (sampling, non-invasive) or pyinstrument. For Go use net/http/pprof or pprof tools.

GPU-specific tracing:
- Nsight Systems (nsys) is the go-to for end-to-end CPU<->GPU timeline. Example: nsys profile --trace=cuda,cublas,osrt -o out --capture-range=cudaProfilerApi --duration=$DURATION -- python -m redwood.serving.worker_main
- nvprof is deprecated for newer CUDA; prefer Nsight. For quick counters: nvidia-smi dmon or nvidia-smi stats via poll.
- NVTX markers: ensure runtime emits NVTX push/pop around kernel-launch boundaries (use redwood-instrumentation crate/module). NVTX greatly helps map high-level ops to kernel spans in nsys.

Generating flamegraphs (offline):
- perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded
- flamegraph.pl out.folded > flame.svg
- We also support speedscope: convert folded to flamescope or use folded->speedscope via tools.

Perf CI job template (gist-like example) — purpose: capture a small canonical workload trace on push to master and fail on new hotspots
- job: perf-smoke-trace
  runs-on: self-hosted-linux-gpu
  steps:
    - checkout
    - run: build artifacts with debug symbols (make debug-build)
    - run: start a minimal worker cluster (docker-compose -f perf-smoke.yml up --detach)
    - run: ./run-smoke-workload.sh --duration 20 --scenario small-context
    - run: ./trace-collect.sh 20 smoke-trace.tgz pod=perf-smoke-worker-0
    - run: ./analyze-ci-trace.sh smoke-trace.tgz --baseline s3://perf-baselines/latest
    - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v2 (upload smoke-trace.tgz and ci-report.html)

analyze-ci-trace.sh (high level):
- Unpack trace, run flamegraph generation, quantify token/sec and top 10 stack hotpaths, compare with stored baseline data. If top-3 stacks increased wall-time by >20% -> fail CI and attach artifacts.
- For GPU hotspots, extract kernel name/milliseconds from nsys report and compare against baseline.

Deeper analysis tips (for performance engs):
- Correlate per-request logs with trace timestamps. Add a tiny tracing header for request IDs so you can pluck exact spans from nsys.
- Check runtime scheduling/affinity: collector shows blocked syscalls (futex, epoll_wait). High futex indicates lock contention—look at batch queue locks and allocator locks.
- Investigate JIT or lazy quantization stalls: first request to a model can trigger kernel compilation or quantize-on-load. Add warmup jobs in perf CI.
- KV cache misses: if traces show repeated cache loads, check serialization/deserialization costs and consider binary cache payloads.

Known gotchas and checklist items before profiling:
- Ensure cgroup/capabilities allow perf and nsys to access perf events and ptrace.
- Disable address space layout randomization if you plan on using dev kernels + addr maps? Generally not recommended for production nodes.
- For containers: run perf with --cap-add=SYS_ADMIN or use privileged helper containers. Keep security team in loop for Private installs.

Example triage timeline (realistic incident):
- 10:02 Alert: p95 latency increased from 160ms -> 420ms for route /v1/generate
- 10:03 Snapshot metrics: GPU utilization 12%, CPU 92%
- 10:05 Run trace-collect.sh 30 -> shows heavy time in tokenization + JSON marshal in sidecar.
- 10:15 Hotfix: switch to optimized tokenizer (switch flag in config), roll out canary - p95 returns to ~180ms
- 10:30 Follow-up: add tokenizer micro-benchmark to perf CI and a pre-warm step for new model deploys.

TODOs / follow-ups:
- Add a flavors of trace-collect.sh for bare-metal Dedicated vs Docker vs K8s (right now we only have k8s script).
- Add a small Java/Node wrapper for services that are not instrumented with /debug/pprof.
- Create a canonical baseline artifacts bucket and a small web UI that surfaces CI trace diffs (speedscope embedded).

References and helpful commands:
- stackcollapse-perf.pl / flamegraph.pl (Brendan Gregg)
- nsys (Nsight Systems) docs and --trace flags
- py-spy / pyinstrument / go pprof
- Example GH PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/2143 (NVTX marker additions)

Notes to self: this doc is intentionally concise/tactical. After initial rollout we should split into:
- Oncall playbook (1 page)
- Perf CI design doc (with thresholds and baselines)
- Deep-dive kernels guide (how to interpret nsys kernel tables for attention/cublas).

If you add scripts, please put them in serving-runtime/tools/perf/ and add small README.md explaining env & IAM for uploading to perf-traces S3.

Unresolved questions:
- What is the acceptable CI runtime cost (GPU hours) for nightly baseline updates? (cc: infra budget)
- Should we keep symbol-stripped builds for dedicated nodes to reduce image size and separately publish debug-symbol artifacts?

Contact for help:
- Aisha (owner) via #eng-perf, Miguel (SRE) for node access, Jing (runtime) for NVTX hooks.

-- end of runbook --
